blocks.text: Atomic spectra are seen when atoms emit or absorb light of particular wavelengths: these are emission and absorption spectra. They are evidence that electrons in atoms can move only between fixed (discrete) energy levels. When electrons absorb energy they move from lower to higher energy levels; the excited electrons then give out energy as they return to lower levels, forming an emission spectrum.

items: An emission spectrum is produced by heating a low-pressure gas. When an electron drops to a lower level it emits a photon whose wavelength matches the energy difference, so the spectrum is a set of distinct coloured lines on a black background.

An absorption spectrum is produced by passing white light through a cool, low-pressure gas. Only photons with exactly the energy needed to excite electrons are absorbed, so the spectrum is a continuous band crossed by dark lines. The dark lines are at the same wavelengths as the bright lines of the emission spectrum of the same element: an absorption spectrum is like a photographic negative of the emission spectrum.

blocks.alt: Top: the hydrogen emission spectrum, coloured lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm on black. Middle: energy levels n = 2 to 6 with arrows from n = 6, 5, 4 and 3 down to n = 2, coloured like the lines. Bottom: the absorption spectrum, a rainbow with dark lines at the same four wavelengths.
blocks.caption: Emission and absorption spectra of hydrogen (original diagram after Figures 29.2 and 29.3).
blocks.long_description: Each visible line of hydrogen corresponds to a jump between level n = 2 and a higher level: 656 nm (red) from n = 3, 486 nm from n = 4, 434 nm from n = 5 and 410 nm from n = 6. A larger energy gap gives a shorter wavelength.
